note: In-session one-vendor panel under D154(b) as amended by D155, run on 2026-10-17 by a Claude Code orchestrating session (Claude Opus 5.5) on dataset 9.4.0, after D167. Three panelists, each stance a separate set of contexts: institutionalist on claude-opus-5-5, bottom_up on claude-opus-5-5, wealth_sceptic on claude-sonnet-5-5, all Anthropic, each through Claude Code subagents. Each panelist answered in batches of ten countries, one fresh context per batch and per round, and the indicator audit in one context per stance, so no context held two stances and none saw another panelist's text except the anonymised round-1 summary the round-2 prompt carries. Two rounds plus the indicator audit, at maxCoverage 1: all nine dimensions for all 125 countries, 1125 country-dimension cells, not the 0.5 ceiling of the 9.0.1 run. Prompts are byte-identical to a gateway run's, built by pnpm bench delphi --in-session with the current prompt version; the system rules were given as a file each panelist read first. Every batch reported it read every prompt in full and wrote every answer by hand. A first attempt the same day stopped at the account's usage limit before any batch finished; its partial answers were discarded and every prompt was regenerated and answered from scratch. No call in this run failed and none was rerun into it. One vendor means the spread measures stance, not vendor, and shared model-family blind spots are hidden by a narrow IQR, which is a floor on real uncertainty (D155). A multi-vendor or gateway run on the same dataset supersedes this one. This is an interpretation layer: its estimates reach only delphiScore and delphiIqr, and blendedScore only where a dimension has no observed indicator; they never enter score.

indicatorJudgements.rationale: Research volume is an output of funding and university systems, closer to Learning than to sensing change. Per-head counts track income and research spending closely, and publication incentives inflate some systems.

A direct reading of an institution that persists, the national statistical system, and a state that cannot see itself cannot anticipate. Part of the score is data openness and dissemination, which rewards well-funded offices, so it is income-tinged.

The core institutional construct: a mandated foresight function with continuity across governments. Build it on mandate, budget line, continuity and documented use in decisions, or a unit that exists on paper will score like one that shapes policy.

A funder committing to a five-year horizon is a real institutional behaviour of patience, but it reads research governance more than anticipation of change in society. Grant registers are uneven across funders, so the definition of a competitive public grant will decide what it measures.

Article volume per head counts output of a formal, funded research sector and tracks university budgets more than any capacity to see change coming. It sees none of the sensing that happens through traders, community networks, diaspora links or local media in poorer countries.

A national statistical system is a real sensing organ, so the C filing holds, but the SPI rewards formal publication standards and administrative registers, which undercount informal economies by design. Several lower-income systems score well on it, so the wealth link is real but weaker than for research output.

A foresight unit's existence and continuity is a direct but narrow, state-centred measure; scoring its mandate will favour countries that copy OECD templates. Anticipation in large informal economies sits in firms, farmers and civil networks that a central unit does not capture, so build it but do not let it stand for the dimension.

Grant duration is a real behaviour of committing to a horizon, but it only observes competitive public funders, which are thin or absent across much of the frame. Poorer funders cannot offer five-year awards whatever their foresight, so the share reads budget security as much as horizon.

Article volume per head is largely a function of funded research capacity and rises with income. It is an input to sensing the future, not anticipation, and does not show a country acting on what it finds.
Statistical system quality is an input to seeing oneself and is closely tied to budget and donor support. Plausible but not anticipation, and it tracks income strongly.

The existence and continuity of a foresight function is a direct, cheap institutional choice that a poor state can make and a rich one can skip. A mandate is not use, so it needs outcome checks. No dataset.

A funder's choice of horizon is behaviour, and the shares sidestep spending levels. Rich systems have grant registers, so coverage will skew wealthy even where the measure itself does not. No data and untried.

Refiled from C to O: registrations are the joint product of individual intention and of a registry that makes formal entry worthwhile, plus tax and offshore-vehicle effects. It reads formal entry rather than agency in general, and it tracks formalisation, which tracks income.

Refiled from C to I: registration time is an institutional condition that lowers the cost of acting, not the action itself. Retirement is correct, because the series is frozen and its successor carries the construct.

Refiled from C to I: it scores the friction a registry imposes, a property of the legal infrastructure that enables agency. Bundling cost into the score brings some income back in, and coverage of 74 of 125 makes it a partial row.

An institutional input, and procedure counts are a fair low-wealth reading of administrative design. Frozen at 2019, it describes the registry of seven years ago, and it overlaps with the B-READY row where both exist.

Refiled from C to O: doing a digital task is an outcome of access, schooling and income, and it is adjacent to Learning more than to turning intention into action. Self-report and a changing task list weaken comparability further.

A felt capacity, not an observed one, and it reads high in autocracies where institutions constrain action most. Response style on 10-point scales and fieldwork years spread over six years make it a weak basis for scoring.

Registered limited liability companies per head count only the intentions that enter the formal register, which is exactly where activity in India, Nigeria or Indonesia is undercounted; I refile it as O, a formalisation outcome. Its variation tracks registry cost and income more than agency.
Registration time is a condition on formal entry, an input, not a measure of people acting; most entrepreneurs in the frame never meet it. The retirement is right.

A score for the time and cost of formal registration is a rule environment, an input to agency, not agency observed; I refile it from C to I. Registration cost is partly relative to income, and the route only matters to those who choose to formalise.
A procedure count is a feature of formal registration law, an input, and frozen at 2019. It overlaps with business entry efficiency as a reading of formal entry friction.

Counting a task done is better than a skill level, but the named tasks (attachments, spreadsheet formulas) are office-PC tasks; mobile money, phone-based selling and messaging-app commerce are how most adults in the frame act digitally. As defined it reads device access and formal work, so the wealth risk is high.

Felt control is a perception, correctly filed, and it has the merit of reaching informal workers equally and tracking income weakly. Response style and high readings in closed autocracies limit what it says about action.

It counts formal limited-liability registrations, so it reads formality and registration regime as much as action; in informal economies it undercounts. It tracks income through formalisation, and is better filed as an outcome than a direct measure.
Retired and replaced; it measured friction in a formal procedure, an input to agency rather than agency. Expert-answered about one standard firm in one city.
A score of regulatory friction, so an input to agency, not agency itself. Rich countries digitise registries and score high; the score blends cost and route, and 74 of 125 are covered.
A count of steps is a legal-design input, frozen at 2019, and an expert answer about a hypothetical firm. It is less wealth-bound than cost but still tracks e-government.
Counting digital acts still follows device and connectivity access, which money buys, and it is self-reported. It sits closer to a skill stock than to turning intention into action; no data now.

A felt capacity, not action, and response style plus regime deference distort it: Vietnam and Nicaragua read high. Its income link is weaker than hard indicators, which makes it a cleaner but noisier signal.

The construct, implementation capacity, is what I care about most, but the measure is aggregated opinion that tracks income. Retirement is correct until observed cross-agency delivery records replace it.
The same perception signal as government effectiveness, and it carries a market-liberal reading of what counts as sound regulation. Retirement is correct.
How global forwarders see a country, which rewards scale and wealth. Retirement is correct; border agency performance survives in the B-READY row.

Several agencies acting together at the border, observed as hours, which is an institutional reading of coordination. Retirement is correct, because it is frozen and its successor carries the construct.

Customs, standards and port agencies working as one system is a fair reading of inter-agency coordination, though it covers one narrow channel. Moving to firm-reported time and cost adds some perception and some income, and it covers only 74 of 125.

The strongest institutional row here: whether finance ministry, legislature and line ministries hold to an approved plan, read from the record. It is a PEFA-type credibility measure, so it also reads fiscal discipline and shock exposure, and a deviation can be a sound response to a shock.
Refiled from C to P: the only source is an executive opinion item. Exclusion is correct; co-authorship between firms and universities in publication metadata would be an observable substitute.

Refiled from C to P: an expert-coded judgement, which the note concedes. It reads associational freedom and regime type at least as much as capacity to organise, so a state that coordinates through formal corporatist channels reads low.

The construct is right if it reads durable joint arrangements with contracts, governance boards and delivery records. Any measure built on PPP finance volume would read capital depth and income, so define it on delivered joint programmes.
An expert and business perception composite that tracks income at 0.91 is a reputation of rich states. The retirement is right.
The same WGI measurement under a different name, and it rewards market-friendly regulation as judged by investors. The retirement is right.

A freight-forwarder survey records how global logistics firms see a country and misses the informal and regional trade networks that coordinate most goods movement in much of the frame. The retirement is right.

Border hours observe several agencies acting together, which is a real if narrow coordination reading for one standard formal shipment. Retired and replaced by the B-READY pillar that carries the same construct.

Border throughput is a coordination act between agencies and firms, and firm-reported time is a step towards experience. It sees only registered traders and none of the cross-border informal trade, and digital trade components push it towards income.

Spending close to the approved plan observes the state coordinating its own actors, and it does not track income tightly. It says nothing about coordination outside government, which is half the question.

As available it is a WEF executive opinion item, so it is a perception, not the C it is filed as. Even observed, it is a narrow formal-sector channel of coordination; exclusion on inspectability is right.

Civil society participation is the closest item on the list to independent actors organising themselves, and it is the one that can see grassroots organisation in poorer democracies. It is expert-coded, so I refile it P; it reads regime openness as much as organising capacity.

Joint delivery of public objectives is a sound construct, but a register of formal partnerships would miss the most common forms in the frame, state work with cooperatives, religious bodies and community groups. Design it to count those or it measures PPP finance by another name.
An aggregate of expert and firm opinion correlating about 0.91 with log income. This is a perception of wealth, and its retirement is right.
The same opinion composite as government effectiveness, relabelled and about equally wealth-bound. Correctly retired.
A forwarder opinion survey that rewards large ports and rich economies. Retired correctly.
Border hours show agency coordination but are an expert answer about one shipment, frozen at 2019. Rich countries have digital customs, so it tracks IT investment as much as coordination.

Throughput of agencies at the border is a fair coordination outcome, but it is a composite score with costs and imports and relies on firm surveys. Digital customs infrastructure is bought; 74 of 125 covered.

The gap between plan and spend is a plain record of alignment, not opinion. It reads conservative budgeting and shock exposure as well, and wealthy states can forecast better, but the link is looser than with governance indices.
An executive opinion item that reflects the respondent's view of the national innovation system and tracks income. Not inspectable and no data.
Expert-coded and tied to the democratic channel, so it reads regime type as much as organising capacity. It is not a direct measure and belongs under P.
Joint delivery of objectives would be a behavioural measure, but PPP databases track financing deals that rich markets host. No dataset.

Rule of law is the institutional foundation of cooperation with strangers, so the construct is right, but this measure is a perception composite that tracks income. Retirement is correct until court records replace it.
Reputation for corruption, not experience of it, and near-duplicate of rule of law. Retirement is correct; bribery incidence carries the experiential side.
Court time to enforce a claim is an observable property of legal infrastructure that lets strangers contract. Retirement is correct, because it is frozen and the successor carries the construct.

The strongest institutional row here: whether courts resolve and enforce commercial disputes, which is what makes trust in strangers rational. The score blends time, cost and reliability, adds some income through cost, and covers only 74 of 125.
Experience of whether the state treats a stranger by its rules, a good reading of administrative integrity. Reticence can make a low value a cautious answer, and the income gradient is real.

Refiled from O to P: it is an expert judgement, though of a specific act. Whether the state obeys rulings it loses is central to institutional trust, but the row reads democracy closely and rewards a state whose courts rarely rule against it.
Reads organised crime and policing, which are adjacent to the dimension, and its variation in this set is mostly income. Retirement is correct.

The standard item, and it tracks institutional quality across countries, but respondents can fill most people with their own circle. It is a perception, so keep it beside the stranger item and do not weight it as a direct measure.

Confidence in institutions reads deference in autocracies, so the battery fails the regime test. Holding it as a check is correct; a valid fill needs an item that does not reward a court that cannot rule against the state.

The best perception item for the construct, because it names the stranger. It is still attitude and not cooperation; an institutional reading would be the use of formal contracts, credit and courts between unrelated parties.

Refiled from O to C: whether courts finish what they start is a direct administrative record of the institution that lets strangers cooperate. Clearance alone hides a growing backlog, so pair it with disposition time, and harmonising case categories across CEPEJ, OECD and national courts is the real cost.
A WGI perception composite of rich-country reputation that correlates with control of corruption above 0.95. The retirement is right.
Reputation for corruption, not corruption, and tied to income. The retirement is right.

Court time is a formal-institution measure for a standard case, and most contracts in the frame are enforced by reputation, networks and informal arbitration. Retired and replaced by the B-READY pillar.

A score of formal court speed, cost and reliability describes the institutional support for trusting strangers, an input, not the cooperation itself; I refile it I. It sees only firms that use courts, so community and customary dispute resolution, which carries trust in much of the frame, is invisible.

A firm's own experience of a bribe request is better than reputation, and it reads whether rules hold with strangers. It covers registered firms only, and reticence plus income correlation keep its validity middling.

Expert coding of government compliance is a judgement, so I refile it P, and at r 0.88 with electoral democracy it reads regime type more than social trust. It says whether the state obeys courts, not whether citizens cooperate beyond their networks.
Homicide reads organised crime and income, and the measured wealth contribution confirms it. The retirement is right.

The most people item is the standard generalised-trust question and reaches informal populations equally, but respondents fill most people with their own circle. It is low across Latin America and Africa where dense network trust supports a lot of cooperation, so it understates distributed capability.
Confidence in institutions reads deference in autocracies and is about the state, not cooperation between strangers. Keeping it as a check is right.

Naming the stranger targets the construct directly and the item reaches informal populations through a household survey. It is still a stated attitude, so a behavioural measure such as informal credit or market exchange with non-kin would be the better long-run target.

Clearance rates are observed records, which I prefer to scores, but they measure formal court throughput, adjacent to trust. Where courts are rarely used, a high clearance rate can mean few cases filed, not trust.
A WGI opinion composite that tracks income and reputation. Correctly retired.
A reputation for corruption and not corruption, correlating above 0.95 with rule of law and closely with income. Retired correctly.
Court time is an outcome of case load and resources and an expert answer about one hypothetical case. Retired and replaced.
A composite score of time, cost and process reliability, which is an outcome of court funding and reform and not trust. Rich countries have funded courts and e-filing; 74 of 125 covered.
Experience-based and so better than opinion, but respondents under-report and low values reflect low reporting as well as clean rules. Correlates with income as strongly as other corruption measures.
Whether the state obeys rulings it loses is a public act, but it is expert-coded, tied to democracy at r 0.88, and feeds WGI rule of law. It reads regime type with a wealth correlate.
Driven by organised crime and inequality, and it raised the wealth correlation of the dimension. It does not measure trust. Retirement is right.

A survey of how much people trust others and a direct reading of the construct, with a looser income link than governance indices. Cultural and survey-mode effects remain, and China reads high on most people.
Confidence in institutions reads deference in autocracies and is not trust beyond personal networks. Low wealth link but it fails on construct. No scorable series.
The stranger-named item is the most precise survey form of the construct and it exposes in-group trust. It is still self-report with format effects, and correlates closely with generalised trust.
Counted from records and not asked, which is good, but it measures court workflow and rich systems can clear by settling. Publisher coverage is split across CEPEJ and OECD. No data.

Refiled from C to O: it reads the result of school and health systems, including child survival and stunting, a stock with a strong income gradient. Learning-adjusted schooling is the valid part, but the last full round is 2020.

Firms as organisations that renew knowledge is the institutional reading I favour, and survey coverage keeps its wealth correlation modest. Coverage skips high-income countries and the item does not distinguish a token induction from a real programme.

The right construct, continuous updating of knowledge, and it reflects adult education institutions and training levies. It exists only for rich countries, so filling it from that source alone would carry income into the dimension.

Reads whether research is used by others, the quality side of knowledge acquisition, but only for the academic system. Whole counting lifts small co-authoring systems, and the unversioned source drifts between fetches.

HCI combines child survival, school years, test scores and adult health, so it is an outcome of public spending and health, not a measure of how a society acquires and updates knowledge; I refile it O. Its strong tie to income and its school-only view miss apprenticeship, informal skills transfer and learning by doing.

Formal training by registered firms is a direct observation of organisations updating skills, and it does not track income tightly. It counts only formal training in formal firms, so on-the-job and informal-sector apprenticeship, the main channel in most of the frame, is invisible.

Adult participation in learning is the closest construct to continuous learning, and non-formal training is in the definition, which I value. As sourced it exists only for rich members; any extension must count community, religious, cooperative and online learning or it will reward course catalogues.

Citation share reads whether elite research is used by other researchers, which is adjacent to national learning and dominated by a small formal sector. Field normalisation and the ratio form dampen wealth somewhat, but whole counting rewards co-authorship with rich systems.
It bundles child survival, schooling and test scores, and so reads health and education spending, an endowment. It is an input to learning and a close proxy for income; the 2020 round is old.

A behaviour of firms updating skills that does not need national wealth, and middle-income countries can exceed rich ones. Survey coverage skips most high-income economies and formal training is a narrow slice.

A direct measure of continuous learning that is cheap to do, but formal provision and surveys are richest in rich states, and non-formal learning is under-recorded elsewhere. Exists for Europe and OECD only.

Whether research is used by others is an outcome, but whole counting lifts small countries and well-funded systems earn citations through networks. It reads research quality more than how a country distributes or updates knowledge.
An outcome of R&D spending and of the patent office as an institution; it records the expensive end of experiments. Filing subsidies and strategic patenting distort it, and it tracks income.
Cheap and frequent, so it is closer to many small attempts, and it depends on an accessible IP office. It also reads branding of existing products and filing fee structures, not only new approaches.

Partly duplicates trademarks and is distorted by subsidies and by the routing of filings to regional offices, which is an institutional artefact, not a capability difference. Keep it only if its correlation with trademarks is below the redundancy threshold.

Cheap attempts, but on one foreign private platform, and coursework and tutorials inflate it. It reads connectivity, English-language developer culture and platform access, which track income, and no national institution stands behind the count.

Refiled from C to O: a first round is an attempt funded with outside risk money, but the count depends on a financial ecosystem and legal infrastructure for equity, which tracks income. Counting deals rather than amounts is the right choice.

Refiled from C to O: TEA counts necessity self-employment the same as a tested venture, so it often reads the absence of formal employment, an institutional failure, as experimentation. It tends to run inverse to income, which disguises its wealth dependence rather than removing it.

An attitude, filtered to people who already see opportunity. The institutional substitute is bankruptcy law: time to discharge, a fresh-start rule and recovery rates are observable and say whether failure is survivable.

The most direct institutional reading of the dimension: a regulator letting firms test under relaxed rules and recording exits. Counting firms through the regime rather than the regime's existence is correct, but the count also reads fintech market size, and regulators define cohorts differently.

Refiled from C to O: spinouts follow from research spending, technology transfer offices and IP ownership rules. Definitions differ by country, and the row reads the research system more than the ease of trying and abandoning approaches.
The make-up of a spending stock that also reads ownership models and the size of total research. Retirement is correct.

Patent filings count experiments that reached a costly legal filing, which is the formal-sector filter I distrust most; frugal and informal innovation never files. Filing strategy and subsidies, as in Korea and China, add noise that is not trying.

Trademarks are cheaper and closer to many small attempts, so this is the better of the IP counts. It still counts only formal firms that register a brand, so informal traders and small producers stay unseen.
Design filings are a registered attempt but they inherit the subsidy and office-routing traps the note lists. They add little beyond trademarks and carry more distortion.

A free, unregistered attempt is the kind of count I want, and it does see grassroots developers in countries such as Nigeria, India and Indonesia. It needs connectivity, a computer and English-language platform habits, so per head it still leans to income and to one platform.

A first venture round counts an attempt only once outside institutional money backs it, which is a formal-finance filter and an outcome rather than the C it is filed as. Most attempts in the frame are funded by family, savings groups and informal lenders.

A household survey that counts every person starting a business, registered or not, is the indicator on this list that sees informal attempts directly. Counting necessity ventures is a feature for this dimension: a necessity venture is still an attempt, though it says less about the ability to abandon and improve.

Fear of failure is an attitude and correctly filed P, but it speaks to the abandon-and-retry part of the question that no count covers. It comes from the same GEM survey as TEA and partly moves with it.

Firms through a sandbox observes the state letting attempts happen, but only for formal fintech-style firms that seek a licence, a narrow slice of experimentation. Many lower-income regulators tolerate testing informally without a sandbox, which this cannot see.
Spinouts count commercialised research from funded universities, an outcome of research spending rather than the C it is filed as, and a tiny formal channel in most of the frame.
The make-up of formal R&D spending is an input stock and misreads ownership models. The retirement is right.
Filing is a costly result of R&D spending and legal support, and it is distorted by state targets and strategic filing. It tracks income through money for lawyers and labs.
Cheaper than patents, but trademarks mark branding and commerce, not trials of new approaches. Registry quality and a formal-business economy lift rich countries.
Subsidy in China and EUIPO filing in the EU distort national counts, and the Netherlands has no series. Partly duplicates trademarks and reads the filing route as much as experiments.
A near-free count of new attempts, which helps, but it needs devices and connectivity and covers one platform, with VPN and student-course noise. Still weaker on wealth than fee-based filings.
First rounds count attempts funded with outside money, which needs deep capital markets and so tracks income. It is an outcome of financial depth, not an experiment itself. No data.

A count of people trying is the least wealth-bound row here, since poor countries show high rates through necessity. It conflates forced self-employment with experiments and gives no value for the attempts.
Attitude to failure among those who see opportunities, a selective sample and cultural response style. Bankruptcy law would be better; wealth link moderate.
Firms moving through a trial regime directly observe permission to try, and cost little. Regimes exist mostly in richer, financialised states, so coverage will skew. No dataset.
A count of spinouts needs research budgets and a transfer office, so it follows income, and definitions are incompatible between countries. No data.
The composition of a spending stock, which is high either where business research is large or where one firm dominates a small system. State ownership distorts it. Retirement is right.
A level of slack, not a speed of response. It mixes labour-market institutions, informality and demography, and a rigid system with a large informal sector can read low.

The closer of the two labour rows to reallocation, because it reads whether displaced workers get re-absorbed through placement services, training and hiring rules. It is ambiguous at low unemployment and depends on survey institutions that record search duration well.

Refiled from C to O: it is the state of a basket, a structural endowment that reflects size and resource luck, and it does not observe a response to change. Concentrated rich exporters and price-driven commodity swings both distort it.

The best row here: observed movement of capital and labour into new lines, normalised by room to enter. It is still an outcome over a 15-year window, so it reads slow structural change better than response to a shock.

The right construct, and it is where state capacity shows most clearly: civil protection agencies, warning systems and recovery authorities that outlast the people in them. Any realistic source mixes in stocks money buys, so wealth risk is high unless the measure is built from observed recovery times.

The most direct institutional reading of adaptability: how fast rules and programmes change through formal channels. Legislative and regulatory timestamps are buildable and less income-bound, but speed must be read beside durability, or churn will score as capability.

Where there is no unemployment insurance, people cannot afford to be unemployed and move into informal work, so low unemployment in poor countries reflects survival reallocation that the rate cannot tell from rigidity. It is a blunt outcome with weak income link and weak construct link.

Duration of unemployment is closer to reallocation speed than the rate, but the note already shows it reads opposite things in tight and slack markets. In informal economies the long-term unemployed are a small formal-job queue, not the population that adapts.

A concentration index is a static product mix, an outcome, not a capacity to switch; I refile it from C to O. It sees merchandise through customs only and misses services, remittance and informal trade buffers that carry adaptation in many lower-income countries.

Entry into new export lines observes reallocation, and the room-to-enter denominator stops a broad basket being rewarded, which keeps wealth risk moderate. It still sees only formal merchandise exports above a million dollars, so domestic and informal reallocation is invisible.

Observed recovery from real shocks is the right construct, and community-level preparedness such as Bangladesh cyclone volunteers shows poor countries can lead here. Any source must observe community warning and recovery, not national plans or stock-based coping indices, or it becomes a wealth measure.

Timestamped rule changes observe the state adapting, but speed of formal rule change misses informal and local adjustment where the law lags practice. Speed is also not quality, so a churning legislature could score well.

A blunt outcome that reads institutional rigidity, informality and demography as much as reallocation. Its income link is moderate but non-monotonic, so the risk lies in misreading it, not in tracking GDP.

Closer to reallocation speed than the headline rate, but it flips meaning between slow and tight markets and survey duration questions differ by country. Rich welfare states score badly and poor informal economies get few recorded durations.

A product mix is a stock, not a capacity to switch, and diversification rises steeply with income while commodity and high-value niche exporters read concentrated for reasons unrelated to fragility. Should be class O, not C.
It observes actual reallocation into new lines and is normalised by room to enter, so it rewards conversion rather than wealth. Goods-only and slow-moving, and a resource find counts as entry.

The only available proxies are INFORM coping capacity, which mixes government self-assessment with purchasable stocks. As filed it is a C aspiration, but any real source would be perception plus wealth; no data now.
Timestamps on rule and programme change would observe the behaviour directly and not depend on income, though rich states legislate more and volume is not quality. No dataset exists.

An economic structure share, driven by development stage, comparative advantage and resource rents. It says little about whether plans become functioning systems and it penalises service economies with strong delivery states.
Reads the product classification of what multinationals assemble, so assembly hubs score high without domestic building capacity. Small exporters swing on a few lines.
A freight-forwarder perception of an infrastructure stock, and stocks track income. Retirement is correct.

An end-to-end delivery by a utility and its regulator, which is execution by institutions at small scale. It is frozen at 2019 and based on one stylised case in the largest business city, so it says little about delivery outside that city.

Accumulated productive know-how, a stock built over decades, so it reads past building more than present capacity. It correlates strongly with income and partly overlaps the export-basket rows in Adaptability.

The most direct measure of state execution: whether procurement, project management and oversight bodies deliver to cost and schedule. Build it on audited ex-post reviews from supreme audit institutions and development banks, with a fixed baseline definition, or optimistic baselines will flatter weak systems.

Refiled from C to O: firm growth is an outcome of finance, contract enforcement and market size, not a direct reading of turning plans into systems. It also needs business registers that most of the frame does not keep comparably.

Manufacturing share of GDP reads economic structure, not execution capability, and it misses the informal workshops and construction that actually build things in large lower-income economies. Its wealth link is weak or hump-shaped, which is its one merit.
The share rewards assembly platforms of multinational firms and says little about domestic building capacity. It overlaps with economic fitness as a reading of export-basket sophistication.
A freight-forwarder perception of infrastructure stock is a reputation measure of rich-country ports and roads. The retirement is right.

An end-to-end delivery time is a genuine small-scale execution measure, but it is the Doing Business standard case of a formal firm in the largest city, so it ignores how most connections are made, off-grid and informal ones included. It is frozen at 2019 and ages every release.

Export fitness reads accumulated productive know-how, which is an outcome of building over decades, and it is strongly tied to income. It only sees goods that cross a border through customs, never domestic or informal production.

Cost and schedule overrun is the most direct execution measure on the list, and rich countries overrun as badly as poor ones, so wealth risk is low. Any build should include subnational and community-delivered projects, not only flagship national programmes.

Firms growing past a threshold observes organisations turning plans into working systems. Registry-based scale-up counts miss informal firms that grow without registering, so a household or establishment survey source would serve the frame better than DynEmp.
An industrial structure share that peaks in middle income and falls in rich service economies, so it is not monotone in wealth but reads sector mix, not delivery. Penalises capable service economies.
Assembly hubs score high without owning design, so it reads trade position as much as building. Its income correlation is moderate, driven by a few electronics assemblers.
A freight-forwarder survey that tracks port size and national wealth. Correctly retired.
End-to-end delivery of a small system is a good building test, but the score is a rescaled expert answer for one city and frozen at 2019. Utilities in rich countries do better, though not uniformly.
Export-basket sophistication is among the best correlates of income and works as an outcome of accumulated capability. It does not separate building from endowment.
Cost and schedule overruns observe execution directly and rich countries overrun too. If it is ever assembled it is the cleanest of the set, though reporting standards will vary. No dataset.
Young firms reaching scale show conversion of plans into systems but depend on market size and capital depth. Coverage is mostly OECD, which would reproduce a wealth split. No data.
Measures the democratic channel by expert and survey opinion, not participation in a common project. Retirement is correct.

The fiscal contract is the most institutional form of shared purpose: citizens fund common goods through a tax authority that collects. Central government only distorts federations, and resource rents and the income gradient of tax capacity confound it; general government tax revenue net of resource revenue would be better.
A structural condition, not a capability, and Gini mixes income and consumption surveys across countries. It belongs beside the dimension as a condition rather than in the score.

Belonging is adjacent to the construct, but any item fails the regime test, because autocracies produce pride and attachment on demand. Keeping it as a gap is correct; a behaviour of belonging is the only defensible fill.

Time given to an organisation is a behaviour of acting for others through durable bodies. Exclusion on inspectability is correct; labour force survey volunteer modules following the ILO manual are the open route.

Expert-coded and unable to separate calm pluralism from suppression. Holding it as a check is correct; a valid fill would need institutional evidence such as peaceful transfers of power or cross-party legislative agreements.

Refiled from C to O: membership is a reported status, not activity, and question format explains part of the spread. It reads the density of a charitable sector, which tracks legal infrastructure for associations and income.
A perception of the democratic channel tracks income and regime type, not whether people see a common project. The retirement is right.

Central tax revenue measures the formal tax base, and countries with large informal sectors collect little whatever people contribute to common goods through zakat, harambee, remittances or community levies. Federal structure and resource rents add noise, so it is close to a measure of formalisation.

Gini is a structural condition, not a capability, and it mixes consumption and income surveys across the frame. Highly unequal societies such as Brazil and South Africa show strong collective action, so the causal claim is weak; I would move it to the conditions.

Belonging is adjacent to the construct but national scale is the wrong level for many in the frame, whose common projects are local, ethnic or religious. Leaving it a gap rather than wiring pride is right.

Giving time is a behaviour of collective action and, in the CAF data I know, poorer countries such as Indonesia and Kenya rank high, so it resists the wealth bias. The item must count informal help to neighbours and not only to organisations, or it repeats the formal-sector filter.
Expert-coded polarisation is a judgement and cannot tell calm pluralism from enforced calm, as the note says. Keeping it a check is right.

Charitable membership is a reported behaviour, but it is membership of a formal organisation, which undercounts mutual aid, rotating savings groups and religious charity; excluding religious membership drops much of the civic life in many lower-income countries. Question-format differences between EVS and WVS add noise.
A perception composite of the democratic channel, which is a different thing from belonging to a common project. Correctly retired.
Tax take rises steeply with income and formal-sector size, and is confounded by federal structure and resource rent. It shows state capacity more than willingness.
A structural outcome that constrains common purpose but is not a capability and varies with region and tax-transfer design. It is not monotone in wealth, so the risk is moderate.
Closer to the construct than anything else but it is self-report and regime-sensitive. No series can fill it now.
A behaviour of acting for others that poor countries show at high rates, so it separates from income. Microdata is proprietary and no data is available.
Hostile polarization bears on shared purpose, but calm can mean a closed regime. Expert-coded and moderately linked to income, and no scorable series now.
Membership in charitable bodies is a reported behaviour that does not need money, but it is membership, not activity, and the question format differs between surveys. Coverage is 37 countries.
